articles.title: Yellow disease, heatwave damage kuruvai paddy in Mayiladuthurai - The New Indian Express
articles.full_text:
According to the Agriculture department, Kuruvai has been cultivated on about 39,400 hectares in the district this season. Photo | Express
MAYILADUTHURAI : Standing Kuruvai paddy crops in Mayiladuthurai have lost their healthy green colour due to an intense heatwave and the spread of yellow disease, leaving farmers worried about heavy yield losses.
According to the Agriculture department, Kuruvai has been cultivated on about 39,400 hectares in the district this season. Farmers said that while those with borewell irrigation in Mayiladuthurai, Kuthalam, Tharangambadi and Sirkazhi blocks raised the crop using pump sets, many others were unable to take up cultivation after the Mettur dam was not opened on June 12 due to inadequate storage, leaving vast stretches of farmland fallow.
“The crops raised during April and May have now reached the heading stage. However, the failure of the expected summer rains, coupled with prolonged high temperatures and hot winds, has triggered widespread incidents of yellow disease and leaf blight in several villages,” said R Anbalagan of the Delta Irrigation Farmers Association.
He also added that the absence of irrigation water from the Mettur dam has added up to the dryness in the paddy fields. “Farmers borrowed money and relied on borewell irrigation to save the crop. But the severe heat and hot winds have caused yellow disease to spread rapidly. With the crop at the heading stage, we fear months of hardwork may go in vain,” said K Ashokan, another farmer.
Agriculture department officials said they had assessed the affected fields and issued advisories to farmers on measures to mitigate the impact of the disease. Officials also added that the affected crops were TPS 5 paddy varieties.

articles.full_text:
Tropical nights post record number so far this summer
A relentless heat wave has pushed Korea to the most nights with temperatures over 25 degrees Celsius (77 degrees Fahrenheit) up to this point this summer.
People beat the heat by dipping their toes in Cheonggyecheon in central Seoul on July 27.
YONHAP
Korea has logged a record number of tropical nights so far this summer as an unrelenting heat wave continues to grip the nation, the state weather agency said Tuesday.
The nationwide average number of tropical nights reached 7.8 between June 1 and Monday, marking the highest figure for the period since 1973, when the country established a nationwide weather observation network, according to the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA).
A tropical night refers to a phenomenon when nighttime temperatures stay above 25 degrees Celcius (77 degrees Fahrenheit).
During that period, the nation's average daily temperature stood at 24.2 degrees — the second highest figure since 1973 — only behind last year's 24.8 degrees.
The weather agency attributed the heat wave to hot and humid air flowing into the country under the influence of the North Pacific High pressure system.
The KMA warned the country is expected to experience hotter weather, with daytime temperatures to range between 33 and 39 degrees from Saturday to Aug. 7.
Daegu is expected to log 39 degrees every day during the weeklong period. The city recorded its all-time high temperature of 40 degrees on Aug. 1, 1942.

PM calls for preemptive measures to minimize heat wave damage
Listen
By Yonhap
Published KST
Prime Minister Han Seong-sook presides over a Cabinet meeting held at Government Complex Seoul, Tuesday. Yonhap
Prime Minister Han Seong-sook on Tuesday called for preemptive measures to minimize damage from heat waves gripping the country, citing forecasts that some regions could see temperatures rise to nearly 40 C.
Han said during a Cabinet meeting that this week could be the culmination of the searing heat and the government should take steps to protect those living in heavily cramped tiny housing units, known as "jjokbang" in Korean, construction workers and other vulnerable people.
"We should check on jjokbang villages, construction sites and other places vulnerable to heat waves in a way that could be seen as excessive," Han said. "In particular, as temperatures in some regions are forecast to rise close to 40 C, this week is expected to be an important culmination."
On Monday, the Korea Meteorological Administration issued the highest heat wave warning for 17 areas in southern Korea.
The serious heat wave warning is the highest warning level established last June, 18 years after the heat wave advisory system was introduced in 2008. It is issued when the highest perceived temperature reaches 38 C or higher, or the maximum daily temperature reaches 39 C or higher, levels considered life-threatening.

Waterlogged roads, knee-deep flooding in busy markets and bumper-to-bumper traffic marked a rain-soaked Tuesday (July 28, 2026) morning in Delhi as heavy showers battered the city, prompting the weather office to issue a red alert for thunderstorms, lightning and rain over the next few hours.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) forecast a generally cloudy sky with heavy rain for the rest of the day, warning of thunderstorms accompanied by lightning and intense spells of rain across the national capital.
Relentless rain through the morning inundated several parts of the city, with waterlogging reported from Connaught Place, Janpath, several roads in Lutyens’ Delhi, Bharat Mandapam Road, Barakhamba Road, Mathura Road near ITO, Kalindi Kunj and other low-lying areas.

Aam Aadmi Party leader Saurabh Bharadwaj posted a video on X from Sadar Bazar, one of Delhi’s busiest wholesale markets, where rainwater had risen to waist level, forcing schoolchildren, office-goers and shoppers to wade through flooded streets.

articles.full_text:
Heavy rainfall swept across Delhi-NCR, including Gurugram, on Tuesday, prompting the India Meteorological Department (IMD) to issue a red alert for the region. The nowcast warning for "extremely heavy rainfall" remains in effect until 3:20 pm.
Videos circulating on social media showed waterlogging in several parts of Gurugram after heavy rainfall. The visuals showed flooded roads, with rainwater accumulating on key stretches across the city.
Traffic movement slows across key stretches
The rain significantly slowed traffic on several of Gurugram's busiest roads during the day. Commuters faced long queues on routes including Sikanderpur, IFFCO Chowk, Ashoka Marg in Sushant Lok Phase 1, and the stretch between Millennium City Centre Metro Station and Bakhtawar Chowk. Traffic also moved slowly on parts of National Highway (NH) 48 towards Manesar, earlier HT reported.
Congestion extended to the Sirhaul border, where vehicles crawled on both carriageways connecting Delhi and Gurugram. Similar conditions were reported on the route from Signature Towers to Tau Devi Lal Complex via Sector 15 Part 2. Old Railway Road leading towards Tau Devi Lal Complex, MG Road towards Sadar Bazar, Sector 9 to Basai village, and the Sector 54-55 Chowk also witnessed heavy traffic snarls.
The impact of the rain was not limited to arterial roads, as several residential neighbourhoods also reported waterlogging. Flooded internal lanes affected local movement, adding to residents' difficulties during the downpour.
Road caved in
In Sector 59, residents reported that a section of a service road near Revenue Road caved in after the heavy rainfall. The incident marks the sixth road cave-in reported in Gurugram during the ongoing monsoon season.
A junior Municipal Corporation of Gurgaon (MCG) official said the matter had come to the civic body's notice and that officials would inspect the site before commenting further.
The IMD has cautioned that heavy spells may continue to trigger waterlogging in vulnerable and low-lying areas. According to the weather department, rainfall activity is expected to weaken from July 30, but heavy rain is forecast to continue over the next 24 hours.

On July 27, Rainfall Recorded in 155 Talukas, Woman Dies Due to Lightning Strike in Panchmahal
Rainfall was recorded in 155 talukas across Gujarat during the last 24 hours. The highest rainfall of around 2.75 inches was reported in Jetpur Pavi in Chota Udaipur district, followed by 2 inches in Limkheda of Dahod district. More than one inch of rain was recorded in 24 talukas.
With five weather systems currently influencing the state, the India Meteorological Department has forecast more heavy rainfall and issued a yellow alert for four districts and two Union Territories for today.
Two women killed in rain-related incidents
The ongoing spell of rain has also claimed two lives. In Ahmedabad, an elderly woman died after being trapped under the debris when a house collapsed late at night.
In a separate incident in Panchmahal district, one of three women struck by lightning succumbed to her injuries. Authorities have urged people to remain cautious as adverse weather conditions are expected to persist.
One woman killed, two seriously injured in lightning strike during farm work
A lightning strike claimed the life of an elderly woman and left two others critically injured while they were working in an agricultural field at Nadarva village in Shahera taluka of Panchmahal district on Monday (27 July) afternoon.
The three women, all from the same family, were planting groundnut crops when lightning struck the field. Sixty-five-year-old Santokben Bamniya died on the spot, while the other two women sustained severe burn injuries.
Injured shifted to Godhra Civil Hospital
The injured women were rushed to Godhra Civil Hospital, where they are undergoing treatment. The incident has cast a pall of gloom over Nadarva village, with residents mourning the loss of a family member in the tragic weather-related accident.
Three women from the same family caught in lightning strike during paddy transplantation, one dies.
Elderly woman killed as rain-weakened house collapses in Ahmedabad
A dilapidated house collapsed late on Monday (27 July) in Mansuri Mohalla of Dagarwad, Dariyapur, after heavy rainfall lashed Ahmedabad, claiming the life of an elderly woman and leaving another person seriously injured.
The incident occurred when the rain-weakened structure gave way, trapping occupants beneath the debris.
Fire brigade rescues victims from debris
After receiving an alert, fire brigade personnel rushed to the spot and launched a rescue operation. Two people were pulled out from under the collapsed structure.
While the elderly woman succumbed to her injuries, the other victim was rescued in a critical condition and rushed to a nearby hospital for treatment. Authorities are investigating the incident as concerns grow over the safety of ageing buildings during the monsoon season.
Pipli–Vataman highway closed, diversion announced for Surat-bound traffic
The Pipli–Vataman Highway in Ahmedabad district has been closed near Pipli village after a rainwater drainage channel was damaged. Authorities have advised motorists to use the Dholera Expressway and the Dhandhuka Highway as alternative routes.
Vehicles travelling towards Surat from Vataman via Pipli have been diverted to the Dholera Expressway. Similarly, motorists heading from Vataman to Dhandhuka have been advised to travel via Dholera.
Heavy rain forecast till August 2; fishermen told to stay ashore
According to India Meteorological Department Director Dr. A.K. Das, fishermen have been advised not to venture into the sea on July 30 and 31 due to adverse weather conditions.
The state is currently under the influence of five active weather systems, including upper-air circulation, two monsoon troughs, cyclonic circulation and a deep depression. These systems have intensified rainfall activity across Gujarat.
Heavy rainfall is expected between July 30 and August 2. A yellow alert has been issued for today and tomorrow (July 28–29) for isolated heavy rainfall in Surat, Tapi, Navsari, Dang, Valsad, Daman, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli.
Active Systems in the state and their impact on rainfall
1. Upper air circulation
- What is it?: When winds start rotating in a circular or spiral pattern slightly above the Earth's surface (typically at a height of 1.5 to 5.8 km), it is called 'Upper Air Circulation'.
- Impact on rainfall: This system pulls moisture-laden winds from the surroundings towards itself. As a result, clouds accumulate and light to moderate rainfall occurs in that area, with locally heavy rainfall in some places. Often this system becomes stronger and transforms into a 'Low Pressure' or 'Cyclonic Circulation'.
2. Monsoon trough
- What is it?: A 'trough' is a long belt of low pressure. During the monsoon, the low pressure line extending from Ganganagar in Rajasthan to the Bay of Bengal is called the 'Monsoon Trough'. If two separate belts or branches (e.g., one in North India and another off-shore trough on the south/west coast) are active, it is called a double monsoon trough.
- Impact on rainfall: The Monsoon Trough is considered the main "highway" for the monsoon. Where this belt passes, moisture-laden winds from the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal converge, resulting in widespread and extensive heavy rainfall. When two troughs are active, the monsoon becomes very active simultaneously across large parts of the state or country.
3. Cyclonic circulation
- What is it?: When winds in the lower or middle levels of the atmosphere start rotating very rapidly in an anti-clockwise direction and a cyclonic circulation develops there, it is called Cyclonic Circulation.
- Effect on rainfall: This system draws abundant moisture from the sea or land. Due to this, a thick cloud cover forms over that area and continuous, heavy to very heavy rainfall occurs. If this system remains stationary over the coast or land for a long time, flood-like situations can arise.
4. Deep depression
- What is it?: Weather systems have a sequence of intensity, such as normal low pressure, well marked low pressure, depression, deep depression, and cyclone. When wind speed reaches between 31 to 61 km/hour and pressure drops significantly, it is called 'Deep Depression'. This is the stage before a cyclone
- Impact on rainfall: This is a very powerful system, it brings with it excessive moisture and cyclonic winds. This system causes extremely heavy to very extremely heavy rainfall. Along with this, wind speed is also very high, which creates emergencies like trees falling down, roads getting blocked, and waterlogging (floods) in low-lying areas.

Delhi on red alert: Heavy rain batters capital, monsoon turns vigorous
A weather system hundreds of kilometres away has flipped conditions over northern India, setting the stage for a prolonged spell of intense rain. Here's what Delhi could see in the near future.
Advertisement
A man rides a bike amid heavy rainfall. (Photo: PTI)
After days of humidity, Delhi-NCR is bracing for one of its most active spells of the monsoon this season, with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issuing a red alert for the national capital as widespread heavy to very heavy rainfall, thunderstorms and lightning are expected over the next 24 hours.
The warning came as a fresh spell of rain began on Tuesday morning, July 28, bringing relief from sultry conditions.
Rainfall was recorded across several parts of the city, with Safdarjung receiving 32.4 mm by 8:30 am, while the Ridge observatory logged 37.6 mm.
WHY HAS DELHI'S MONSOON INTESIFIED?
The current spell is being driven by a deep depression that developed over the northwest Bay of Bengal before moving inland across eastern India.
The system has strengthened the monsoon trough, which is a broad belt of low pressure that stretches across northern India during the rainy season.
As the trough shifts closer to Delhi, it channels moisture-laden winds from the Bay of Bengal into northwest India.
The moist air rises, cools and condenses into towering rain clouds, triggering widespread showers and thunderstorms.
Meteorologists say such systems often produce narrow but intense rain bands, resulting in sharp variations in rainfall across different parts of Delhi-NCR.
This marks a notable turnaround after earlier weeks of relatively scattered rainfall, when the monsoon trough remained away from Delhi, leaving the city humid despite cloudy skies.
MORE RAIN AHEAD FOR DELHI-NCR
The IMD expects the active monsoon phase to continue through Wednesday, with heavy to very heavy rainfall likely over Delhi and adjoining parts of Haryana.
Thunderstorms accompanied by lightning and gusty winds may occur at isolated places, while temperatures are expected to remain below recent highs due to persistent cloud cover and rain.
The renewed monsoon activity also reflects a broader weather pattern unfolding across northern India, where the strengthened monsoon trough and the Bay of Bengal weather system are expected to sustain widespread rainfall over the coming days.
While the showers are likely to bring much-needed relief from heat and humidity, they could also disrupt daily life as the capital experiences one of its strongest monsoon spells this July.

Delhi-NCR rain forecast, July 28: Heavy rain lashes Delhi, Noida, Gurugram; ‘Orange alert’ in place as more showers predicted over next 48 hrs
Temperatures across Delhi, Gurgaon, Noida, Ghaziabad and Faridabad are expected to remain in the low to mid-30s degrees Celsius, while humidity levels are likely to stay high, creating warm and humid conditions.
Heavy rain lashed several parts of Delhi-NCR on Tuesday morning, bringing much-needed relief from the recent spell of heat and humidity. The showers, accompanied by cloudy skies and gusty winds, affected normal life in several areas, with waterlogging and slow-moving traffic reported on key roads. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued an Orange Alert for parts of Delhi, warning of moderate to heavy rainfall, thunderstorms and strong winds. The alert covers North, Central, East, West, North-West, North-East Delhi and Shahdara, where intense rain is expected at isolated places.
According to the IMD, the wet spell is likely to continue over the next 48 hours, with intermittent rain expected across Delhi, Noida, Gurugram, Ghaziabad and Faridabad. The weather department has advised residents to remain cautious during thunderstorms, avoid waterlogged areas and expect traffic disruptions during peak hours.
Delhi’s base weather station at Safdarjung recorded 32.4 mm of rainfall till 8:30 am. Other stations also received significant rainfall, with Ridge recording 37.6 mm, Lodhi Road 36.7 mm, Ayanagar 4 mm and Palam 0.8 mm.
The rainfall has led to a noticeable drop in temperatures. Delhi recorded a minimum temperature of 25.5 degrees Celsius, which was 1.8 degrees below normal. Daytime temperatures are expected to remain around 32-34 degrees Celsius, making conditions much more comfortable than in recent days.
The IMD has forecast that the monsoon will remain active over northwest India, keeping skies mostly cloudy and bringing frequent spells of rain through Wednesday. Thunderstorms with lightning and gusty winds are also likely during this period.
Humidity made Monday uncomfortable
Even though a few areas witnessed brief spells of rain on Monday, the weather remained hot and sticky. The heat index touched 49 degree celsius, making it feel much hotter than the actual temperature because of the high humidity. By around 5.30 pm, the heat index was still close to 48 degree celsius.
The maximum temperature settled at 38.1 degree celsius, around 3.2 degrees above normal, while the minimum temperature was 28.6 degree celsius, about 1.3 degrees above normal. Humidity levels stayed very high, ranging between 76 per cent and 100 per cent, adding to the discomfort.
Today’s Weather Forecast
According to the IMD, Tuesday and Wednesday will remain cloudy, with light rain expected at many places and moderate showers likely in some areas. Earlier, a Yellow Alert has been issued for both days, warning of rain, thunderstorms and gusty winds. The spell of rain is likely to continue on Thursday as well, although the IMD has not issued any weather alert for that day.
The increased rainfall is expected to bring down daytime temperatures by 5-6 degrees Celsius, making the weather much more pleasant across the city.
Today, the maximum temperature is expected to remain around 33 degrees celsius, while the minimum may be close to 24-25 degrees celsius. Cloudy skies are likely throughout the day, with intermittent spells of light to moderate rain, thunderstorms and gusty winds expected across Delhi, Noida, Gurugram and Ghaziabad.
Similar weather conditions are expected, with cloudy skies, light to moderate rainfall and a further dip in daytime temperatures.
Delhi Airport issues weather advisory as rain continues across NCR
Delhi’s Indira Gandhi International (IGI) Airport has issued a travel advisory after the weather department forecast rain and adverse weather conditions in and around the national capital.
Airport authorities said flight operations are currently running as scheduled, despite the ongoing rainfall. However, they added that teams on the ground are closely coordinating with airlines and other agencies to minimise any weather-related disruptions and ensure smooth airport operations.
Passengers have been advised to check the latest flight status with their respective airlines before leaving for the airport, as changing weather conditions could lead to delays or schedule changes later in the day. Rain and thunderstorms are expected to continue across Delhi and the NCR, according to the IMD.
